lessonTitle: Cardiovascular and Respiratory Pathology: Infarction, Airway Disease and Lung Inflammation

blocks.text: A 64-year-old man dies suddenly on day 5 after a heart attack. At autopsy the left ventricular wall at the infarct is soft, yellow-tan and has torn, filling the pericardial sac with blood. The pathologist can date the infarct to within a day or two from the slide alone. How?

blocks.title: Myocardial infarction
blocks.text: Myocardial infarction (MI) is death of cardiomyocytes caused by prolonged ischaemia, most often from thrombus on a ruptured atherosclerotic plaque in a coronary artery. Coagulative necrosis means the cell outline (ghost architecture) is preserved for days because proteins denature and enzymes are inactivated, so the tissue stays firm at first.

blocks.markdown: **Timeline.** Changes before about 4 hours are invisible on routine light microscopy (electron microscopy shows irreversible injury after about 20 to 40 minutes), and nothing is visible grossly until roughly 12 hours, although a tetrazolium chloride (TTC) stain shows dead muscle as an unstained pale area from about 2 to 3 hours because dehydrogenase enzymes have leaked out. Neutrophils arrive first, macrophages next, then granulation tissue (new capillaries and fibroblasts), and finally collagen.

rows: Usually normal (TTC stain shows pale area from 2 to 3 hours)
Usually normal; waviness of fibres at the edge may appear
Early coagulative necrosis, oedema, haemorrhage, wavy fibres
Hypereosinophilic cytoplasm, pyknotic nuclei, early neutrophil margin
Dense neutrophil infiltrate, loss of cross-striations and nuclei
Neutrophils die; macrophages clear necrotic fibres
Early granulation tissue with new capillaries at the edge
Dense collagen scar with few cells
blocks.caption: Approximate chronology of myocardial infarction (times vary with reperfusion and infarct size).

blocks.title: Dating an infarct from a histology slide
blocks.prompt: A section from the edge of a left ventricular infarct shows necrotic myocytes being engulfed by macrophages. Neutrophils are sparse and a thin rim of capillaries and plump fibroblasts is present at the periphery. Estimate the age and the physical state of the wall.

steps.text: Neutrophils dominate at 1 to 3 days and then die off, so sparse neutrophils mean the infarct is past the first few days.
Macrophages removing necrotic fibres are typical of days 3 to 7 and continue into the second week.
A rim of new capillaries and fibroblasts is early granulation tissue, which first appears at 7 to 10 days.
Combining these, the macrophage-rich phase overlapping with early granulation tissue places the infarct at about 7 to 10 days.

blocks.answer: About 7 to 10 days old; the wall is at its softest because necrotic tissue has been removed but little collagen has yet been laid down.

blocks.markdown: Complications track the timeline. **Arrhythmia** is greatest in the first hours. **Fibrinous pericarditis** appears at about 2 to 3 days when inflamed necrotic muscle reaches the epicardium. **Free wall rupture** (causing haemopericardium and tamponade) is most likely at 3 to 7 days, when necrotic muscle has been digested by macrophages but granulation tissue has not yet strengthened it. **Ventricular aneurysm** develops over weeks to months as a thin fibrous scar bulges.

**Chronic airway disease.** Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) comprises emphysema and chronic bronchitis. Both obstruct airflow but by different pathological mechanisms. In **emphysema** there is permanent enlargement of airspaces distal to the terminal bronchiole with destruction of alveolar walls and without obvious fibrosis. Elastic recoil is lost, so small airways collapse during expiration. In **chronic bronchitis** the airways are narrowed by mucus gland hypertrophy, goblet cell hyperplasia, chronic inflammation and fibrosis.

blocks.title: Chronic bronchitis and the Reid index
blocks.text: Chronic bronchitis is a clinical diagnosis: productive cough on most days for at least 3 months in each of 2 consecutive years, after other causes are excluded. Histologically the Reid index is the thickness of the submucosal mucous gland layer divided by the thickness of the bronchial wall (epithelium to cartilage). Normal is below about 0.4; values above about 0.5 indicate gland hypertrophy.

blocks.latex: \text{Reid index}=\frac{\text{gland layer thickness}}{\text{wall thickness (epithelium to cartilage)}}
blocks.caption: Both thicknesses are measured in the same units (mm), so the index is dimensionless.

rows: Anatomical: airspace enlargement with wall destruction
Clinical: chronic productive cough (3 months, 2 years)
Large airspaces, fragmented septa, no fibrosis
Gland hypertrophy, goblet cell hyperplasia, inflammation, fibrosis
Centriacinar (smoking, upper lobes); panacinar (alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, lower lobes)
Protease-antiprotease imbalance; loss of elastic recoil
blocks.caption: Emphysema versus chronic bronchitis. Many patients have both.

blocks.title: Calculating a Reid index
blocks.prompt: A bronchial wall in a long-term smoker measures 2.5 mm from epithelium to cartilage. The mucous gland layer measures 1.6 mm. Calculate the Reid index and interpret it.

steps.text: Substitute the measurements, both in millimetres.
Compare with the reference: above about 0.5 indicates gland hypertrophy consistent with chronic bronchitis.

blocks.answer: The Reid index is 0.64, which is raised and consistent with chronic bronchitis.

blocks.markdown: **Pneumonia and fibrosis.** In pneumonia, alveoli fill with inflammatory exudate. In **lobar pneumonia** (classically pneumococcal) a whole lobe is consolidated and passes through four stages: congestion (days 1 to 2, vascular engorgement and proteinaceous fluid), **red hepatization** (days 2 to 4, red cells, neutrophils and fibrin fill alveoli), **grey hepatization** (days 4 to 8, red cells lysed, fibrin and neutrophils remain) and resolution (macrophages clear debris). **Bronchopneumonia** is patchy, centred on bronchi and bronchioles, with neutrophils in airways and surrounding alveoli. **Interstitial (atypical) pneumonia** shows lymphocytes and macrophages within alveolar septa rather than in airspaces.

**Pulmonary fibrosis** is replacement of alveolar tissue by collagen. The prototype is **usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP)**, the pattern of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: patchy subpleural and basal fibrosis, **fibroblastic foci** (small clusters of proliferating fibroblasts), and **honeycomb change** (cystic spaces lined by bronchiolar epithelium). Old scar sits next to young foci, a feature called temporal heterogeneity. The lung becomes stiff and gas transfer falls.

blocks.title: Link time to mechanism
blocks.text: In MI each stage follows from what cells are doing: neutrophils at one to three days, macrophages by one week, granulation tissue by ten days, scar by two months. Rupture risk peaks when necrosis is cleared but scar is not yet formed.

points: MI evolves from coagulative necrosis with neutrophils (1 to 3 days) through macrophage clearance and granulation tissue to a collagen scar, and rupture risk peaks at 3 to 7 days.
Emphysema destroys alveolar walls without fibrosis; chronic bronchitis shows mucous gland hypertrophy and a raised Reid index.
Lobar pneumonia fills alveoli with neutrophils and fibrin; pulmonary fibrosis (UIP) shows subpleural fibroblastic foci and honeycombing.

questions.stem: A section of infarcted ventricle shows coagulative necrosis with a dense infiltrate of neutrophils and no granulation tissue. Which age is most consistent?

options.text: Less than 4 hours
1 to 3 days
7 to 10 days
More than 2 months

distractorRationale.a: Light microscopy is usually normal at this stage and neutrophils have not arrived.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: neutrophils peak at 1 to 3 days.
distractorRationale.c: By this time macrophages and granulation tissue predominate.
distractorRationale.d: A scar would be collagenous and sparsely cellular.

questions.explanation: Neutrophils infiltrate from about 12 to 24 hours and peak at 1 to 3 days, before dying off. The absence of granulation tissue excludes a later infarct.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman collapses 6 days after an anterior MI and has jugular venous distension with muffled heart sounds. Why is rupture most likely at this time?

options.text: Necrotic muscle has been digested by macrophages but granulation tissue is not yet established
Dense collagen has formed and made the wall brittle
Neutrophils have just begun to arrive and are releasing proteases
Reperfusion injury occurs at exactly 6 days

questions.correctOptionText: Necrotic muscle has been digested by macrophages but granulation tissue is not yet established

distractorRationale.a: Correct: this is the period of maximal softening.
distractorRationale.b: Collagen scar strengthens the wall and appears later.
distractorRationale.c: Neutrophil infiltration is earlier, at 1 to 3 days.
distractorRationale.d: Reperfusion injury is not time-locked to day 6.

questions.explanation: Between days 3 and 7 macrophages remove dead myocytes, leaving a weak wall before granulation tissue and collagen strengthen it. Rupture into the pericardium gives tamponade, matching raised venous pressure and muffled heart sounds.

options.text: Permanent enlargement of airspaces distal to the terminal bronchiole with destruction of walls and without obvious fibrosis
Productive cough for 3 months in 2 consecutive years
Collagen replacement of alveolar septa with honeycombing
Neutrophil exudate filling alveoli of a whole lobe

questions.correctOptionText: Permanent enlargement of airspaces distal to the terminal bronchiole with destruction of walls and without obvious fibrosis

distractorRationale.a: Correct: this is the anatomical definition.
distractorRationale.b: This is the clinical definition of chronic bronchitis.

questions.explanation: Emphysema is defined anatomically, not clinically. Wall destruction without fibrosis removes elastic recoil and tethering of small airways.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old never-smoker has dyspnoea and CT showing lower-zone predominant panacinar emphysema. Which mechanism is most likely?

options.text: Unopposed neutrophil elastase from alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
Chronic mucus hypersecretion from smoke irritation
Deposition of collagen by fibroblastic foci
Bacterial lobar consolidation

questions.correctOptionText: Unopposed neutrophil elastase from alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency

distractorRationale.a: Correct: lack of the inhibitor allows elastase to destroy alveolar walls.
distractorRationale.b: This is the mechanism of chronic bronchitis, not early panacinar disease in a non-smoker.
distractorRationale.c: This is pulmonary fibrosis, not emphysema.
distractorRationale.d: This is infection, not a chronic emphysema mechanism.

questions.explanation: Panacinar emphysema with lower-zone predominance in a young non-smoker points to alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. Centriacinar emphysema from smoking favours the upper lobes.

questions.stem: At autopsy a consolidated lower lobe is firm and grey. Alveoli are packed with fibrin and neutrophils, and red cells are largely lysed. Which stage is this?

options.text: Congestion
Red hepatization
Grey hepatization
Resolution

distractorRationale.a: Congestion shows vascular engorgement and fluid, not firm grey lung.
distractorRationale.b: Red hepatization has numerous intact red cells in alveoli.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: red cells lysed with fibrin and neutrophils remaining.
distractorRationale.d: Resolution shows macrophages clearing debris and softening of the lung.

questions.explanation: Grey hepatization (days 4 to 8) follows red hepatization once red cells are lysed. The fibrin and neutrophil-filled alveoli give the firm, pale lung.

questions.stem: Fibroblastic foci and subpleural honeycomb change are characteristic histological features of usual interstitial pneumonia.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: UIP is patchy, basal and subpleural fibrosis with fibroblastic foci and honeycombing. These features distinguish it from inflammatory pneumonias.

questions.stem: A bronchial wall section from a patient with chronic productive cough measures 1.5 mm from epithelium to cartilage, and the mucous gland layer measures 0.9 mm. Calculate the Reid index (dimensionless).
questions.explanation: Reid index equals gland thickness divided by wall thickness, 0.9 / 1.5 = 0.6. This is above the about 0.5 threshold, supporting gland hypertrophy.

questions.stem: A patient with COPD has FEV1 1.4 L and FVC 3.2 L after bronchodilator. Calculate FEV1/FVC as a percentage. An obstructive pattern is a ratio below 70%. (Answer in %.)
questions.explanation: FEV1/FVC = 1.4 / 3.2 = 0.4375, or 43.75%. This is well below 70%, indicating airflow obstruction as expected in emphysema or chronic bronchitis.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old has fever with a patchy lung shadow on the right, while a 68-year-old has progressive dyspnoea, basal crackles and a subpleural reticular shadow. Contrast the expected histology of bronchopneumonia and usual interstitial pneumonia.
markingGuide: Bronchopneumonia: patchy distribution centred on bronchi and bronchioles
Neutrophils and exudate in airways and surrounding alveoli
UIP: patchy subpleural and basal fibrosis
Temporal heterogeneity of old scar and new foci
Fibrosis is of the interstitium whereas pneumonia fills airspaces
questions.explanation: Bronchopneumonia is an exudative airspace disease from bacterial infection, while UIP is interstitial scarring. Marking should reward the distribution and the cell or tissue type in each.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man is reviewed 2 weeks after an inferior MI. Explain the sequence of cellular events that converts the necrotic myocardium into a scar and why the wall is weakest between days 3 and 7.
markingGuide: Coagulative necrosis of myocytes from ischaemia
Macrophages clear dead myocytes from day 3 onward
Granulation tissue from about 7 to 10 days
Collagen deposition and scar after weeks
Weakest when necrosis is removed but granulation tissue and collagen are not yet present
questions.explanation: The scar forms because adult cardiomyocytes do not regenerate effectively. Debris must be cleared before repair, and the gap between clearance and collagen deposition explains the vulnerable period.
